vignette: Sara, a 56-year-old woman of Oceania descent, has been working in social ministry for over three decades. Her life was turned upside down two years ago when she experienced a traumatic sexual assault at her workplace during an outreach event. The event shattered what had once been a vibrant and fulfilling career. The assault left Sara with intense triggers that are now deeply woven into the fabric of her daily existence. She is particularly triggered by familiar faces, especially related individuals within her church community, who remind her of the people present on the day of the incident. These reminders often force her to retreat from social interactions and maintain a guarded demeanor. Sara has also found that moments of happiness and relaxation now serve as potent triggers. The memory of feeling safe and content before the assault is a stark contrast to what followed, making these feelings particularly dangerous for her. Her body reacts with intense discomfort whenever she begins to relax, leading her to avoid situations where such emotions might arise. Her maladaptive strategies have developed over time in response to these triggers. She feels an overwhelming need to stay near exit points at all times, a behavior that has become especially noticeable during community events and gatherings. This constant vigilance is coupled with the urge to eat excessively when she experiences distress; food becomes both a comfort and a way to distract herself from her thoughts. Heavy makeup also serves as a coping mechanism for Sara. She feels safer in public when heavily made up, believing that it makes her less noticeable and therefore less vulnerable. This routine has become an integral part of her daily life, even extending into her professional duties at the social ministry where she interacts with clients and community members. Sara's body remains perpetually on high alert. She experiences a constant sense of tension and hypervigilance, which is only exacerbated by her triggers. Her memories of the assault are vivid and intrusive, replaying as if in a film that plays over and over again whenever she is triggered or feels uncomfortable. The clarity and detail of these memories have made it nearly impossible for Sara to escape them. They force their way into her mind at inappropriate times, often during moments when she least expects it, like while working with clients or attending church services. This uncontrolled access to the memory has led to a vicious cycle where her maladaptive strategies become more entrenched and her threat perception intensifies. Sara's negative appraisals further complicate this cycle. She believes that someone else should have stopped the assault from happening and that there is something fundamentally wrong with her as a person. These beliefs fuel her sense of inadequacy, making it difficult for her to trust others and leading her to overeat or retreat into heavy makeup even more frequently. Her perception that she is no longer capable of doing what defined her professionally has led to withdrawal from many social ministry activities she once enjoyed. This erosion of confidence feeds back into her triggers, making the assault-related memories even more intrusive and vivid. What finally brought Sara to seek help was a series of events where these maladaptive strategies began to take a toll on her relationships and work. She found herself increasingly isolated from her husband and colleagues at the social ministry. The constant checking of locks and exits has strained her professional commitments, leading to concerns about her reliability and focus. Sara is most afraid that she will never regain control over her life and that she will continue to be plagued by these overwhelming triggers and memories. She hopes for a way to find peace with herself and her past experiences without allowing them to dictate every aspect of her present life.
